In so far as the structures are more weather-tight and energy inefficient equipment is repaired or replaced with more efficient equipment, this program will result in a lower energy consumption rate.
During the process of maintaining and restoring of structures, opportunities are frequently presented to reduce the long-term energy requirements of the structure. These should not be overlooked in this program. Since about 53 percent of house energy use is for space heating and since it is estimated that 45 to 50 percent of space heating energy use is usually wasted, the improvement of space heating efficiency alone can result in a considerable reduction of overall home energy use. The best way to improve heating efficiency is by insulation of the structures. When units have attics (as opposed to flat roofs), ceiling insulation can be installed with relative ease. Further, when flat roofed structures are being re-roofed it is sometimes necessary to remove the old roof, presenting an opportunity to install ceiling insulation, if none exists. Installation of wall insulaltion is probably not cost effective unless either the interior or exterior surface of the wall is removed for other reasons such as termite repair work. In such cases, the opportunity to place wall insulation should not be passed, even if it does not involve all of the exterior walls of the structure. Insulating glass (Thermal plane) should be used for window replacement. Weatherstripping on all windows and doors should be installed. If new furnaces are installed (in the rehabilitation program) they should be gas heaters, and all duct work which passes through uninsulated portions of the structure should be insulated. Such energy conservation measures taken while performing other rehabilitation or conservation projects on a home could result in a substantial (up to 30 percent) energy savings in the long term for the affected structures. In addition, such measures will make the structures less expensive to operate, which also benefits the homeowner.
Other energy conservation measures which should be considered during the process of maintaining or rehabilitating a structure include the following measures. All replacement refrigerators and water heaters should be selected for their low-energy consumption. Space heaters should be controlled with a clock-operated thermostat which provides a day and a night setting. All chimney flues should have a tight damper. New gas-using appliances such as stoves and furnaces should be of the type which utilize electric starters instead of pilot lights. All hot water pipe runs should be as short as possible and hot water pipes which pass through uninsulated portions of the structure should be insulated. When windowless bathrooms are improved, an exterior, insulated glass window should be installed rather than an electric fan which uses electric energy to send heated air outside. Home occupants should receive information about how to conserve energy in home operation.
